name: Image Upload & Delivery Pipeline
tagline: From a synchronous resize in the request to signed uploads, workers and a global CDN
summary: Every product that lets users upload a photo eventually builds this pipeline. The naive version — accept the file in the request, resize it there, write it next to the app — works on the first day and fails in four distinct ways: request latency, disk, availability and bandwidth. The mature version moves bytes out of the request path entirely, does transformation asynchronously in idempotent workers, stores originals in object storage, and serves derived variants from an edge cache. Each step keeps the previous design and adds only what the new bottleneck demands, with the storage-versus-compute trade-off recurring at every stage.
requirements: A user uploads an image and the request returns in well under a second, even for a 20 MB photo from a phone.
Each image is available in several sizes (thumbnail, feed, full) plus a modern format, without the client knowing how they are produced.
Uploaded images are durable: losing a worker, a server or a disk must never lose an original.
Processing is retried on failure and a retry must not produce duplicate or corrupted variants.
Images load quickly for users on every continent, and image bandwidth must not flow through application servers.
Uploads are scanned for malicious content and unacceptable material before an image becomes publicly visible.
Replacing an image at the same logical URL takes effect for all viewers within minutes.

steps.title: Resize inside the upload request
steps.scale: 1,000 users · a few uploads per minute
steps.problem: Nothing has broken yet — this is the starting point. A user posts a multipart form, the handler needs a thumbnail and a display size, and the simplest correct thing is to do all of it before responding.
steps.why: One handler receives the bytes, validates the type and dimensions, produces two derived sizes with an image library, writes all three files to the server's local disk under a generated key, and inserts a row pointing at them. It is chosen because it is a hundred lines of code with no queue, no bucket and no second failure domain, and at a few uploads per minute the CPU cost is invisible. But this design is the canonical example of work that does not belong in a request: decoding and re-encoding a 20 MB photo takes seconds of CPU, so the user watches a spinner while a request-handling thread is pinned; a burst of ten concurrent uploads saturates the worker pool and slows every unrelated endpoint on the same process; a failure at the final step leaves the earlier variants orphaned on disk with no row to find them by; and a timeout or a lost connection forces the user to re-upload the whole file. The storage-versus-compute trade-off appears here for the first time in its simplest form: we spend compute once and store the results forever, which is the right default when a variant is read many times, and the wrong one for a variant nobody ever requests.

nodes.label: Browser / App
nodes.why: POSTs the original file and waits for the response before it can show the image.

nodes.label: App Server
nodes.why: Does everything synchronously; the request occupies a thread for the entire decode and re-encode.

nodes.label: Local Disk
nodes.why: Files sit next to the application, so the server is now stateful and its disk is a single point of data loss.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Owns the metadata row: owner, key, dimensions and the paths of the derived files.

steps.title: Accept fast, transform in queued workers
steps.problem: Upload latency and blast radius both became unacceptable. p95 on the upload endpoint is several seconds and p99 is a timeout; every marketing push produces a burst that pins CPU on the API servers and degrades login and feed requests that share the process; and a failed resize means the user's upload is simply lost, because there is nothing to retry from.
steps.why: Split acceptance from transformation. The request now does the minimum that must be synchronous — authenticate, sniff the content type, cap the size, write the original once, insert a row with status 'pending' — and returns 202 with an image id. A job goes onto a queue and a separate pool of workers decodes the original and produces the variants. This is the rule the rest of the design is built on: never resize in the request path, because transformation is CPU-bound and unbounded in duration while a request handler is a scarce, latency-sensitive resource; separating them lets the two scale independently, so a backlog becomes a delay in variants appearing rather than a site-wide slowdown. Workers must be idempotent, because at-least-once delivery means a job can be redelivered after a timeout or a crash: variant keys are derived deterministically from the original's content hash plus the transform parameters, writes are conditional on the key not existing, and the metadata update is a compare-and-set on the status column — so processing the same job three times produces exactly the same bytes and one state transition. Failures retry with exponential backoff and land in a dead-letter queue after a bounded number of attempts, where a human can inspect an image that no decoder accepts. The costs: variants are eventually consistent, so every client needs a placeholder state; a queue and a worker fleet are new things to operate and monitor by queue depth and age; and originals still live on a server disk, which is the next thing to break.

nodes.label: Browser / App
nodes.why: Gets 202 and an image id immediately, then shows a placeholder until the variants are ready.

nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.why: Upload requests are now short and uniform, so plain round-robin works and one slow upload no longer hurts a whole instance.

nodes.label: Upload API
nodes.why: Does no image decoding at all; its only expensive act is streaming the original to storage rather than buffering it in memory.

nodes.label: Job Queue
nodes.why: Absorbs upload bursts as backlog; depth and oldest-message age are the two metrics that tell you whether workers are keeping up.

nodes.label: Transform Workers
nodes.why: Idempotent by construction: variant keys are content-hash plus parameters, writes are conditional, and the status update is a compare-and-set.

nodes.label: Dead-letter Queue
nodes.why: Bounds retries so a corrupt file cannot spin forever, and keeps the evidence for inspection.

nodes.label: Shared File Storage
nodes.why: Must now be reachable by both API and workers, so local disk becomes a network volume — durable enough for today and the bottleneck of the next step.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Holds pending/ready/failed per image; the status column is the idempotency guard for redelivered jobs.

steps.title: Object storage behind a CDN, with on-the-fly variants
steps.problem: Bandwidth and storage both hit a wall. Serving images through the API means image bytes saturate application network interfaces and every view burns a request handler; the shared volume needs manual expansion and its backups take longer than a day; users far from the region wait seconds for a photo; and the product keeps inventing new sizes, so a redesign means re-processing 40 TB of originals to add one more variant nobody may look at.
steps.why: Move the bytes to storage designed for them and serve them from the edge. Originals and variants go into object storage, which is effectively unlimited, durable across availability zones, cheap per gigabyte and — the decisive property — directly serveable, so a CDN can use the bucket as its origin and application servers leave the delivery path entirely. Objects are addressed by content hash and are therefore immutable, which lets the CDN cache them with a very long TTL and makes a cache hit the normal case; the origin sees only misses. The second change is where the storage-versus-compute trade-off gets an explicit answer instead of a default: rather than precomputing every size, an image service in front of the origin derives variants on request from the original and writes the result back to storage, so a new size costs one transformation the first time somebody asks for it and zero afterwards. Precompute the two or three sizes that are always needed on the upload path, derive the long tail lazily — that keeps storage proportional to what is actually viewed while keeping the CDN hit rate high. Requests are signed or restricted to an allow-list of parameter combinations so nobody can use the resizer as free compute. The costs: an extra system in the miss path with its own cold-start latency, a bill that shifts from storage to compute for rarely viewed sizes, and the loss of local-filesystem semantics — object storage has no rename, no partial write and eventual visibility for listings, so code that assumed a POSIX volume must change.

nodes.label: Browser / App
nodes.why: Asks for /img/<hash>/w=640 and never learns whether that variant already existed.

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.why: Content-hash URLs are immutable, so variants are cached at the edge for a year and the origin only ever sees first requests.

nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.why: Now carries JSON and upload requests, not image delivery — the traffic mix that broke it is gone.

nodes.label: Image Service
nodes.why: Reads the original, applies an allow-listed transform, returns it and writes it back to storage so the next miss is a plain object read.

nodes.label: Upload API
nodes.why: Unchanged from step 2, but writes originals to the bucket instead of a shared volume.

nodes.label: Job Queue
nodes.why: Now only for the two or three sizes worth precomputing on upload; everything else is derived lazily.

nodes.label: Transform Workers
nodes.why: Same idempotent, content-addressed writes; a redelivered job overwrites identical bytes at an identical key.

nodes.label: Object Storage
nodes.why: Durable, effectively unlimited and directly serveable as the CDN origin; lifecycle rules move cold originals to a cheaper tier.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Stores the content hash and processing state; it is never on the image delivery path.

steps.title: Signed uploads direct to storage, with async scan and transform
steps.problem: The upload path is the last place image bytes still flow through the application. Every upload occupies an API connection for the duration of a phone's slow cellular transfer, so a few thousand concurrent uploads exhaust connection limits and cost bandwidth twice — in and back out to storage; large files force long request timeouts that mask real failures; and there is still no scanning, so a malicious or unacceptable file becomes publicly reachable the moment its variant is derived.
steps.why: Take the bytes out of the request path completely. The client asks the API for a short-lived signed upload URL scoped to one object key, content type and maximum size; it then PUTs the file straight to object storage, optionally in parts with resume, and the API is involved only in two small JSON calls. Bandwidth cost halves, API connection counts collapse and a dropped upload is retried by the client against the same key without re-involving the backend. Because the write no longer passes through code, the storage bucket emits an object-created event that becomes the trigger for the rest of the pipeline: a scan step (content-type verification by magic bytes, decompression-bomb limits, malware and policy classification) runs before anything is published, and only after it passes do transform jobs run and the metadata row flip to visible. Uploads land in a quarantine prefix that the CDN cannot read, so nothing is deliverable until it is cleared. Idempotency matters more than ever here, because storage event delivery is at-least-once and can duplicate or reorder: the object key is the job's natural idempotency key, every step is a compare-and-set on the image's state, and a re-delivered event for an already-published image is a no-op rather than a second publish. The costs: orphaned objects when a client gets a signed URL and never uploads (a lifecycle rule expires the quarantine prefix), a genuinely asynchronous product state that the UI must show honestly, signed-URL parameters that must be tightly scoped or they become an open upload endpoint, and a scanning step that adds seconds of latency and its own false-positive appeal path.

nodes.label: Browser / App
nodes.why: Two small API calls plus a direct multipart PUT to storage that it can resume itself after a network change.

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.why: Reads the public prefix; quarantined objects are unreachable from the edge by bucket policy, not by convention.

nodes.label: Upload API
nodes.why: Signs a URL scoped to one key, content type, size cap and a few minutes of validity, then records an expected-upload row.

nodes.label: Object Storage
nodes.why: Receives bytes directly from clients and emits an object-created event; a lifecycle rule expires unclaimed quarantine objects.

nodes.label: Event Stream
nodes.why: Replayable, multi-consumer log so scan, transform and notification stages are independent and can be re-run after a fix.

nodes.label: Scan Workers
nodes.why: Runs before publication: magic-byte checks, pixel and decompression limits, malware and content classification; failures never reach the public prefix.

nodes.label: Transform Workers
nodes.why: Triggered only after a clean scan; keys stay content-addressed so a duplicate event rewrites identical bytes.

nodes.label: Image Service
nodes.why: Unchanged from step 3; only ever reads from the public prefix.

nodes.label: Dead-letter Queue
nodes.why: Terminates retry loops for files no decoder accepts and for scan failures that need human review.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: expected → uploaded → scanned → published, each transition a compare-and-set so at-least-once events cannot double-publish.

steps.title: Multi-region storage with invalidation on re-upload
steps.problem: Two problems arrived together. Uploads are still directed at one region, so a user on another continent pushes a 20 MB photo across an ocean and a regional storage outage stops uploads worldwide. And the immutability assumption finally broke: the product now lets a user replace an avatar or a product photo at a stable URL, and because that URL is cached at the edge for a year with a content-independent key, viewers keep seeing the old image — while purging every variant of every replaced image on every edge is neither instant nor free.
steps.why: Regionalise the write path and make replacement an explicit, versioned operation. Signed upload URLs are issued for the bucket nearest the client, so bytes travel a short distance and a regional failure only affects uploads in that region; buckets replicate asynchronously to a second region for durability and for read failover, and the metadata database gets regional read replicas with writes still going to one primary — because the image state machine needs a single serialisation point far more than it needs local write latency. The invalidation problem is solved primarily by design rather than by purging: internal object keys remain content-addressed and immutable, and a stable public URL resolves through a small, cheap indirection — an alias record mapping logical id to the current content hash, cached at the edge for seconds rather than a year. Replacing an image writes new immutable objects and updates the alias, so viewers converge within the alias TTL and no variant ever has to be purged. Explicit CDN purge is kept as the exception path for legal takedowns and mistakes, issued per logical id, treated as best-effort and asynchronous, and rate-limited because purges are metered and slow. The costs: cross-region replication is an ongoing bandwidth and storage bill for data most users never read in the second region, replication lag means a just-uploaded original may be briefly missing at the failover origin, one write primary means upload metadata writes still pay a cross-region round trip for distant users, and the alias indirection adds a short-TTL lookup to the delivery path — a real latency and request cost accepted deliberately in exchange for never needing a global purge on the normal path.

nodes.label: Browser / App
nodes.why: Presign returns a URL in the closest region; reads go to the CDN with a stable logical URL that survives replacement.

nodes.label: Global CDN
nodes.why: Caches immutable variants for a year and the logical-to-hash alias for seconds, so a replacement propagates without purging any variant.

nodes.label: Geo DNS / Anycast
nodes.why: Sends API and presign calls to the closest healthy region and is the failover switch when one region is unhealthy.

nodes.label: Regional Upload API
nodes.why: Runs in every region; signs URLs for its own bucket so upload bytes never cross an ocean.

nodes.label: Alias Store
nodes.why: The indirection that replaces purging; tiny, read-heavy, replicated per region and cached at the edge with a short TTL.

nodes.label: Object Storage — Region A
nodes.why: Receives direct uploads from nearby clients and is the CDN origin for that region.

nodes.label: Object Storage — Region B
nodes.why: Asynchronous cross-region replication for durability and read failover; lag means a very recent object may not be there yet.

nodes.label: Event Stream (replicated)
nodes.why: Same log as step 4, replicated across regions; the alias update is just another consumer of the publish event.

nodes.label: Regional Workers
nodes.why: Run where the bytes are, so transformation never pulls a large original across regions; still idempotent and content-addressed.

nodes.label: Purge Service
nodes.why: Issues per-logical-id CDN purges for takedowns and mistakes only; rate-limited, asynchronous and monitored because purges are metered and slow.

nodes.label: Metadata: primary + replicas
nodes.why: One write primary keeps state transitions serialisable; regional read replicas serve lookups, accepting replication lag on reads.

edges.label: point logical id at new hash

textAlternative: Five diagrams show an image pipeline growing. Step 1: a client posts a file to one app server that validates, resizes and writes originals and variants to local disk, recording a row in PostgreSQL. Step 2: the request only stores the original and enqueues a job; separate idempotent transform workers produce variants, retry with backoff and dead-letter permanent failures, while the client polls a pending status. Step 3: originals and variants move into object storage with a CDN in front, and an image service derives long-tail variants on a CDN miss and writes them back, so application servers leave the delivery path. Step 4: clients upload directly to storage with short-lived signed URLs into a quarantine prefix; an object-created event drives scan workers, then transform workers, and each state transition is a compare-and-set so at-least-once events cannot double-publish. Step 5: uploads are signed for the nearest region with cross-region replication, and a stable public URL resolves through a short-TTL alias mapping a logical id to the current content hash, so replacing an image converges without purging immutable variants; an explicit purge service remains for takedowns.
